::: {.bnr-cheat-sheet .bnr-cheat-page--git}

::: {.bnr-cheat-heading}
::: {.bnr-cheat-heading__label}
QUICK REFERENCE
:::

Use this page for routine Git work on the BNR Info-Hub. The VS Code and
PowerShell routes operate on the same repository and can be used together.
:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-rule}
**Never edit on `main`.** Start with a clean working tree, update local `main`,
then create a short development branch. Only a reviewed pull request should
merge a development branch into protected `main` on GitHub.
:::

## Git primer

::: {.bnr-cheat-panel}

Git keeps a history of the public Info-Hub source on your computer. GitHub holds
the shared copy, where BNR can review changes and merge them into `main`.

| Term | Plain meaning | In the BNR Info-Hub |
|---|---|---|
| **Git** | The version-control system on your computer. It records changes to files over time. | It records public-safe code, documentation and website source. It must never hold confidential data, tokens or private workflow files. |
| **GitHub** | The shared online copy of the repository. | It is where branches are reviewed through pull requests and where the protected `main` branch is updated. |
| **Branch** | A separate working line for one change. | Create one before editing. It keeps unfinished work separate from the live-site branch. |
| **Stage** | Select the exact file changes that will go into the next saved checkpoint. | Stage only the public-safe files that belong to the current task. |
| **Commit** | A named saved checkpoint on your local branch. | It records one focused, reviewed change but does not send it to GitHub or change the website. |
| **Push** | Send the commits on your branch to GitHub. | It makes the branch available for review. It does not change `main` or deploy the website. |
| **Pull** | Bring changes already on GitHub into your local copy. | Pull updated `main` before starting a new branch and after a pull request is merged. It is not a pull request. |
| **Pull request and merge** | A request to combine a reviewed branch with another branch; merging accepts it. | A pull request into `main` is the only normal route for a website change to join the protected branch. |
| **GitHub Actions and deployment** | The automated online build and publication process. | A merge into `main` starts the Quarto build and deployment. Check the Actions run and then the live page. |

:::

## Routine branch-to-deployment route

::: {.bnr-cheat-panel}

### 1. Check, update and branch before editing

Use this before starting any new change to make sure you work from the latest
approved version without editing `main`.

| Task | VS Code route | PowerShell / CLI route |
|---:|---|---|
| Check the current position | Open **Source Control**. Check the branch name in the lower-left status bar and investigate every listed change. | `git status`<br>`git branch --show-current` |
| Move to `main` | Click the branch name and select `main`. Stop if unexplained local changes prevent the switch. | `git switch main` |
| Update local `main` | In **Source Control**, select **… > Pull**. Confirm that no merge conflict appears. | `git pull --ff-only origin main` |
| Create the working branch | Click the branch name, select **Create new branch**, and enter a short task name such as `fix-report-link`. | `git switch -c fix-report-link` |
| Confirm before editing | Check that the status bar now shows the new branch. | `git branch --show-current`<br>`git status` |

`--ff-only` allows a straightforward update but stops rather than creating an
unexpected local merge when local `main` has diverged from GitHub.

:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-grid .bnr-cheat-grid--two .bnr-cheat-grid--git-card-gap}

::: {.bnr-cheat-panel}

### 2. Review the change

Use this after editing to check exactly what you changed before saving it in
Git.

**VS Code**

1. Open **Source Control**.
2. Read the complete **Changes** list.
3. Select each file to inspect its before-and-after diff.
4. Confirm every file is public-safe and belongs to this task.

**PowerShell / CLI**

```powershell
git status
git diff --check
git diff
```

`git diff --check` identifies whitespace errors. A successful command normally
prints nothing.

:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-panel}

### 3. Stage and commit only intended files

Use this when the change is ready to record and you want the commit to contain
only the files for this task.

**VS Code**

1. Select `+` beside each intended file.
2. Check the **Staged Changes** list.
3. Enter a short commit message and select **Commit**.

**PowerShell / CLI**

```powershell
git add path/to/first-file path/to/second-file
git diff --staged
git commit -m "Describe the focused change"
```

Prefer named paths to `git add .`. Only staged changes enter the commit.

:::

:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-grid .bnr-cheat-grid--two .bnr-cheat-grid--git-card-gap}

::: {.bnr-cheat-panel}

### 4. Push the development branch

Use this after committing to place the development branch on GitHub for review.

**VS Code:** select **Publish Branch** for its first push, or **Push** after
later commits on the same branch.

**PowerShell / CLI — first push**

```powershell
git push -u origin fix-report-link
```

**Later pushes from the same branch**

```powershell
git push
```

Pushing the branch stores the proposed change on GitHub. It does not change
`main` or the live website.

:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-panel}

### 5. Merge the approved change on GitHub

Use this when the branch has been checked and is ready to join the protected
`main` branch.

1. Open the BNR Info-Hub repository on GitHub.
2. Create a **pull request** with `main` as the base and the development branch
   as the compare branch.
3. Review the changed-file list and required tests.
4. Complete any required BNR review.
5. Select **Merge pull request** only when the change is approved.

**Pull** updates a local repository. A **pull request** proposes that GitHub
merge reviewed branch changes into `main`.

:::

:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-grid .bnr-cheat-grid--two .bnr-cheat-grid--git-card-gap}

::: {.bnr-cheat-panel}

### 6. Confirm deployment

Use this after the pull request is merged to confirm that the updated website
was built and made live successfully.

A merge into `main` starts the **Publish Quarto site** GitHub Actions workflow.
It installs the declared dependencies, renders the site and deploys the result.

On GitHub:

1. open **Actions**;
2. open the newest **Publish Quarto site** run;
3. confirm both build and deploy succeeded; and
4. check the affected live page, listing and download.

A local render, commit, branch push or approved analytical publication does
not by itself deploy the website.

:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-panel}

### 7. Update local `main` after the merge

Use this after GitHub has merged the branch so your local `main` contains the
same approved change.

First confirm that the development branch has no uncommitted work. Then:

```powershell
git status
git switch main
git pull --ff-only origin main
git branch -d fix-report-link
```

In VS Code, use the branch selector to return to `main`, select
**Source Control > … > Pull**, then delete the merged local branch only when it
is no longer needed. GitHub may separately offer **Delete branch** for the
merged remote branch.

:::

:::

## Compare branches, commits and files {.bnr-cheat-print-page-break}

::: {.bnr-cheat-grid .bnr-cheat-grid--two}

::: {.bnr-cheat-command-panel}

### Compare the current branch with GitHub `main`

Use this when you want to see everything the current branch would add to the
latest `main` branch on GitHub.

In VS Code, open **Source Control Graph** to inspect the branch and its commits.
Select a commit to see its changed files and open a file in the diff editor.

For an exact branch comparison:

```powershell
git fetch origin
git diff --stat origin/main...HEAD
git diff origin/main...HEAD
git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD
```

The first command refreshes knowledge of GitHub. The other commands show the
files changed, their exact differences and the commits the branch would add.

:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-command-panel}

### Compare two commit hashes

Use this when you want to see exactly what changed between two known points in
the repository history.

In **Source Control Graph**, locate a commit by its short hash, select it and
open its changes. Use the commands below when the comparison must be exactly
between two named commits:

```powershell
git diff --stat OLDER_HASH NEWER_HASH
git diff OLDER_HASH NEWER_HASH
git diff OLDER_HASH NEWER_HASH -- path/to/file
```

Use the last command when only one file matters. These commands inspect history;
they do not alter any file or branch.

:::

:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-panel}

### Reinstate one file from an older commit

Use this when a current file needs to be replaced by a known earlier version
without moving the whole branch backwards.

Start from updated `main` and create a development branch using the routine
route above. Do not restore directly on `main`.

| Task | VS Code route | PowerShell / CLI route |
|---:|---|---|
| Find the earlier version | Open the file, expand **Timeline** in Explorer and select earlier Git entries to inspect their diffs. | `git log --oneline -- path/to/file` |
| Reinstate the selected version | After confirming the hash, open **Terminal > New Terminal** and run the exact restore command. | `git restore --source=OLDER_HASH -- path/to/file` |
| Review the result | Open **Source Control** and inspect the file’s diff against the current branch. | `git diff -- path/to/file` |
| Keep the reinstatement | Test it, then stage, commit, push and merge it through the normal pull-request route. | Use the normal `git add`, `git commit` and `git push` sequence. |

This copies the named file version into the current development branch. It does
not move the branch backwards or rewrite Git history.

:::

## Small recovery commands

::: {.bnr-cheat-grid .bnr-cheat-grid--three}

::: {.bnr-cheat-rule-card}
**Unstage a file but keep its edits**

Use this when you staged a file by mistake but want to keep its local changes.

VS Code: select `−` beside the file under **Staged Changes**.

`git restore --staged -- path/to/file`
:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-rule-card}
**Discard one uncommitted edit**

Use this when you are certain that one file's uncommitted changes should be
removed.

VS Code: right-click the confirmed file and select **Discard Changes**.

`git restore -- path/to/file`

This removes that working-tree edit. Check the exact path first.
:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-rule-card}
**Wrong change already merged**

Use this when a problem is found only after the change has entered `main`.

Create a correction branch from current `main`, correct or restore the source,
test it and merge another pull request. Do not rewrite `main` history.
:::

:::

## Rules to retain

::: {.bnr-cheat-grid .bnr-cheat-grid--rules}

::: {.bnr-cheat-rule-card}
**Keep private material out of Git.** Never stage confidential data, tokens,
private paths, staging packages, logs, approvals or review evidence.
:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-rule-card}
**Inspect before staging.** Stop when `git status` shows an unexplained or
unrelated file. Do not hide it inside the current commit.
:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-rule-card}
**Do not bypass protected `main`.** Do not push directly to `main`, force-push,
rewrite shared history or merge an unreviewed branch.
:::

::: {.bnr-cheat-rule-card}
**Stop on conflicts.** Do not guess through a diverged `main`, merge conflict,
methodological uncertainty or possible disclosure problem.
:::
